There are two common causes for a failure-to-fire, both primer related. The first is that the primers might be seated a bit high, so that it is only when the firing pin strikes them, that they are driven down into the correct position. This robs the firing pin of some the energy normally used to deform the primer and set it off.

The other likely possibility is that the primers are hard, made of a tougher, thicker material. This can be a quality control error or it might be the result of using primers that were intended for a military application.

In either case, you'll see a shallow firing pin impression, instead of the deep impression you would normally see. If the primers were high, you could probably detect the resulting change in height by rubbing a fingertip over the base of the casing, and comparing what you feel to the feel of an unused round.

Most should fire if they are run through the pistol again. Some guns will be more sensitive to this than others, but of course if you have a really bad batch of ammo it will fail to fire in just about any gun.

If they fail to fire on the next attempt, then there is something really wrong, maybe bad primer compound or no compound at all.
